title: Job 4:1–11
context: Job 4:1–11 begins the first speech of Eliphaz the Temanite, the first of Job’s three friends to answer Job’s lament in chapter 3. Teman is often associated with Edom (compare Genesis 36:11), a region known for wisdom, though the connection is not certain. Eliphaz begins gently, reminding Job that he has strengthened others and asking whether his piety should not be his confidence. Then he asks who ever perished being innocent, and he argues from his own observation that those who plow iniquity reap trouble and perish by the breath of God. These are Eliphaz’s words, not the book’s verdict. The narrator has already called Job blameless and upright (1:1), and the LORD later says that the three friends did not speak what is right about him as Job did (42:7). Both traditions recognize that much of what Eliphaz says about God’s justice is true in general, but they also see that he misapplies it by assuming Job’s suffering must be caused by his sin.

verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz the Temanite answers, beginning the first round of speeches. Arminian readers see him as a sincere friend who came to comfort Job (2:11), though his words will show the limits of his understanding of Job’s suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the book introduces his speech as his own answer to Job, not as God’s word. Both traditions read the verse in light of 42:7, where the LORD rebukes the three friends for not speaking what is right.

verses.text: “If someone ventures to talk with you, will you be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks whether Job will be grieved if someone speaks, but says no one can keep silent. Arminians see Eliphaz trying to begin gently, while also showing that he feels compelled to correct Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the tension between his concern and his urge to answer Job’s lament. Both traditions read his opening as courteous in tone, while recognizing that his speech is his own perspective, not the book’s verdict.

verses.text: Behold, you have instructed many, you have strengthened the weak hands.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz reminds Job that he has instructed many and strengthened weak hands. Arminian readers see a true acknowledgment of Job’s past faithfulness in helping others, which agrees with the narrator’s description of Job (1:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the praise as genuine. Both traditions note that Eliphaz is using Job’s past counsel to set up a challenge, and they read the verse as Eliphaz’s words, not the book’s assessment.

verses.text: Your words have supported him who was falling, you have made the feeble knees firm.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job’s words have supported those who were falling and strengthened feeble knees. Arminians see Job’s past ministry of encouragement, which makes his present distress all the more painful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of supporting the weak as a picture of godly counsel. Both traditions read the verse as part of Eliphaz’s introduction, preparing for his suggestion that Job should take his own advice.

verses.text: But now it has come to you, and you faint. It touches you, and you are troubled.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says that now trouble has come to Job, and he faints and is troubled. Arminian readers see some truth in the observation that it is harder to bear suffering than to counsel others, but they also sense a lack of compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the remark as implying that Job should apply his own counsel. Both traditions note that Eliphaz does not yet understand the depth of Job’s loss, and they read the verse as his words.

verses.text: Isn’t your piety your confidence? Isn’t the integrity of your ways your hope?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks whether Job’s piety and integrity should not be his confidence and hope. Arminians see a reminder that a righteous person should trust God, and they note that this is true in general.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Both traditions note that Eliphaz seems to suggest that if Job is truly upright, he has nothing to fear, a view the book will challenge, since Job’s suffering did not come from a lack of integrity (1:8; 2:3).

verses.text: “Remember, now, who ever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks who ever perished being innocent, or where the upright were cut off. Arminian readers see a claim that is true as a general pattern of God’s justice but is not true in every case, and they note that the book shows Job suffering though innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that this is Eliphaz’s view, not the book’s doctrine. Both traditions read the question in light of the LORD’s verdict in 42:7 and the opening chapters, which show the righteous can suffer.

verses.text: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble, reap the same.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says that from what he has seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. Arminians see a principle found elsewhere in Scripture (compare Galatians 6:7), but they note that Eliphaz bases it on his own observation and applies it too broadly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the principle is true in general. Both traditions note that Eliphaz uses it to imply that Job’s suffering must be the harvest of his sin, a conclusion the book does not support.

verses.text: By the breath of God they perish. By the blast of his anger are they consumed.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the wicked perish by God’s breath and are consumed by the blast of his anger. Arminian readers see a true statement of God’s judgment on the wicked, which Scripture affirms in many places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power over life and death. Both traditions note that Eliphaz’s point is true about God, but that he is using it to suggest Job is among the wicked, which the book rejects.

verses.text: The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions, are broken.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the roaring and teeth of the lions are broken. Arminians see a poetic picture of the powerful wicked being brought low, a common image in wisdom literature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the lions as a figure for violent or proud people. Both traditions note that the image may also hint at Job’s own loss of his household, though this is Eliphaz’s implication, not the narrator’s statement.

verses.text: The old lion perishes for lack of prey. The cubs of the lioness are scattered abroad.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the old lion perishes for lack of prey and the lioness’s cubs are scattered. Arminian readers see the image completing the picture of the wicked losing their strength and their families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Many interpreters note that the scattered cubs may be a painful allusion to Job’s children, and both traditions read the image as part of Eliphaz’s argument, which the book’s verdict does not endorse.
